add_eyes.name: Theodor Herzl
add_eyes.role: Feuilleton (arts and literature) editor of the Neue Freie Presse, aged 37 in 1897; playwright, and founder of political Zionism
add_eyes.side: Viennese liberal press; the Zionist movement
add_eyes.where: The Neue Freie Presse editorial office, Vienna; often travelling (The Hague, Constantinople, Palestine)
add_eyes.vantage_label: the editor who chose what the city read
add_eyes.authenticity: Herzl kept his diary from 1895 until shortly before his death in 1904. It was first published in three volumes as Theodor Herzls Tagebücher (Jüdischer Verlag, Berlin, 1922–23), with some passages left out at first. The complete critical edition is in Briefe und Tagebücher (Propyläen, 1983–96). His notes to Schnitzler survive at Cambridge University Library and are in the digital Schnitzler letters edition. Digested here, not quoted.
add_eyes.bio: Herzl ran the arts pages of the paper the Secession argued with, and he took or refused Schnitzler's fiction, so his desk is where Viennese art turned into newsprint. His diary hardly mentions the Secession. It is about Zionism, emperors and his employers Bacher and Benedikt, who would not let the movement into their paper. That silence shows how differently the same street could look from the newsroom.

sources.title: Herzl to Schnitzler, 8 May 1900 (Schnitzler letters edition)

add_eyes.name: Adolf Fischer
add_eyes.role: Collector of East Asian art, then in his early forties, based in Berlin; later founder of Cologne's Museum of East Asian Art
add_eyes.where: His collection on the walls of the Secession, Vienna, January–February 1900
add_eyes.vantage_label: the lender who explained Japan to Vienna
add_eyes.authenticity: His explanation of ukiyo-e aesthetics is in the catalogue of the 6th Secession exhibition. His book Wandlungen im Kunstleben Japans (Berlin, B. Behr, 1900, with decorations by Wada Eisaku) is cited in Bahr's essay on the show. Neither is a diary. They are dated public texts.
add_eyes.bio: Fischer lent the whole of the Secession's sixth exhibition, its only show given over to a single non-European tradition. He was then in Japan in 1900–01, where he introduced the Secession artist Emil Orlik to a Tokyo art association. His view is the collector's: Japan as a living art, not a souvenir.

sources.title: The Vienna Secession: exhibitions and catalogues (6th exhibition)
Schirn Mag: Emil Orlik, Japan and the colour woodcut

add_eyes.name: Emil Orlik
add_eyes.role: Prague-born painter and printmaker working in Vienna, aged 29 when he left for Japan
add_eyes.where: Yokohama, Tokyo and Nikko, spring 1900 to February 1901

waypoints.label: Back towards Vienna, end of February 1901

add_eyes.vantage_label: the Viennese artist who went to the source
add_eyes.authenticity: Orlik wrote letters and postcards from Japan, chiefly to the print scholar Max Lehrs. They are quoted in the Schirn Kunsthalle's material on him. A complete published edition was not checked here. Digested, not quoted.
add_eyes.bio: While Vienna looked at Fischer's prints in the Secession, Orlik went to Japan to learn colour woodcut from Japanese craftsmen. He was disappointed by the westernised ports and drawn to the old crafts. He brought the technique back to Vienna and Berlin, and his letters are the return leg of the January 1900 show.

sources.title: Schirn Mag: Art for All, Emil Orlik, Japan, colour woodcut

add_entries.headline: Sketching a building, architecture the art that moves him
add_entries.digest: Herzl drew up a plan for a Jewish house in Basel, a meeting hall for the Zionist congresses, and noted in passing that architecture was the art that spoke to him most. That same year Olbrich's Secession building was going up on the Karlsplatz. The diary does not mention it. His architecture belonged to a movement, not to a style.
add_entries.source_note: Theodor Herzls Tagebücher, vol. 2 (1923), entry headed 10 Juli, falling between the entries for 5 May and 31 July 1898 (scan at archive.org). Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: In the Dutch painter Israëls's studio, talking Zionism
add_entries.digest: On his way to London, Herzl called on the old Dutch painter Jozef Israëls and spent the visit explaining Zionism to him. For the feuilleton editor of Vienna's leading paper, a studio visit had become a recruiting call. Six weeks later the Secession's new building opened without him.
add_entries.source_note: Theodor Herzls Tagebücher, vol. 2 (1923), entry 1 Oktober [1898], Haag. Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: Back at the paper after Jerusalem: smiles and envy
add_entries.digest: Back from Palestine, where the Kaiser had received him on 2 November and committed to nothing, Herzl found that his action committee had done little in his absence. At the Neue Freie Presse his colleagues smiled instead of laughing, some envied him, and Benedikt asked sourly what the Kaiser had said about Austria. The entry was written six days after the Secession building opened a short walk away, and it says nothing about it.
add_entries.source_note: Theodor Herzls Tagebücher, vol. 2 (1923), entries 2 November (Jerusalem) and 18 November [1898], Wien. Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: Japan fills the Secession: the sixth exhibition opens
add_entries.digest: The Secession's sixth exhibition opened, given over entirely to Japanese art from Fischer's collection: woodblock prints, paintings and objects. In the catalogue Fischer explained the aesthetics of ukiyo-e for a Viennese public that knew Japan mostly as decoration. It ran until 25 February and was the worst-attended Secession show so far. Six weeks later the same rooms held Klimt's Philosophy.
add_entries.source_note: Dates and attendance: The Vienna Secession exhibitions and catalogues page (6th exhibition, 20 January to 25 February 1900). Fischer's catalogue text: Schirn Mag on Orlik.

add_entries.headline: Bahr on the Japanese show: shamed by Japan's restraint
add_entries.digest: In his essay on the Japanese exhibition, Bahr argued that Japanese art had freed European painters since the 1860s by doing without shadow, perspective and illusion. It sharpened their sense of colour and left the viewer's imagination to finish the picture. He admired its unity of man and nature and said its restraint put Europe to shame. Then he turned to politics: Japan, modernising after its revolution, now had Europe's troubles too, and a nation should borrow foreign achievements only to express its own nature.
add_entries.source_note: Bahr, 'Japanische Ausstellung', in the section on the 6th exhibition in his collection Secession (1900; preface dated Easter 1900), Kritische Schriften VI, ed. Pias/Schnödl (bahr.univie.ac.at PDF). The essay cites Fischer's Wandlungen im Kunstleben Japans (1900). Original newspaper and day not confirmed.

add_entries.headline: Landing at Yokohama and disliking the modern veneer
add_entries.digest: Orlik reached Yokohama in the spring and wrote home that the port was covered in an ugly modern veneer, not the Japan of the prints he had come for. About a month later he moved to Tokyo to look for printmakers and carvers. The country Vienna had just seen on the Secession's walls was already changing under his eyes.
add_entries.source_note: Schirn Mag, 'Art for All: Emil Orlik, Japan, colour woodcut' (letter to Max Lehrs; arrival in spring 1900). Day not given.

add_entries.headline: A one-line ask for the Pentecost number
add_entries.digest: In the weeks after the Philosophy scandal, Herzl wrote Schnitzler a short note on the paper's letterhead asking whether he would write something for the Pentecost number. The editors would be very glad of it. Schnitzler sent nothing, and the supplement appeared on 3 June without him. It is the feuilleton editor's ordinary work, a few lines in blue ink.
add_entries.source_note: Herzl to Schnitzler, 8 May 1900, Schnitzler letters edition L03871 (Cambridge University Library). Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: Offering Herzl a story that cannot be cut
add_entries.digest: Schnitzler wrote to Herzl offering a story for the Christmas number. It ran to about nine columns and could not be shortened, and he thought the Neue Freie Presse supplement its proper place. In the same letter he apologised for a remark at Aussee that Herzl had heard about through Beer-Hofmann, to clear up a needless misunderstanding. The edition links the letter to Leutnant Gustl, though the letter itself does not name the story.
add_entries.source_note: Schnitzler to Herzl, 15 November 1900, Schnitzler letters edition L03937. Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: Has Herzl even received Gustl?
add_entries.digest: More than a fortnight after sending the manuscript, Schnitzler wrote again to ask whether Herzl had received Lieutenant Gustl and whether he could print it uncut. Three weeks later the officer's monologue was in the Christmas paper, and within months it cost its author his own reserve commission.
add_entries.source_note: Schnitzler to Herzl, 3 December 1900, Schnitzler letters edition L03935; Schnitzler Chronik, 3 December 1900. Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: Complaining that the fee ignored Gustl's length
add_entries.digest: Three weeks after publication Schnitzler wrote to Herzl again. An earlier letter seemed to have gone astray, though the editors note Herzl did receive it. He asked whom to approach about his fee, because the payment had ignored the story's unusual length despite his warning. The novella that shook the army was, at the newspaper, a question of columns and honoraria.
add_entries.source_note: Schnitzler to Herzl, 14 January 1901, Schnitzler letters edition L03940 (Central Zionist Archives, H1:1926-6). Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: A letter from the shrines of Nikko
add_entries.digest: Orlik wrote from Nikko, the mountain shrine town north of Tokyo, during months spent studying Japanese woodblock printing. Through Fischer, also in Japan, he had been introduced to a Tokyo art association and allowed to show his work there. A Viennese artist was being judged by Japanese eyes.
add_entries.source_note: Schirn Mag on Orlik: letter sent from Nikko in mid-September 1900; Fischer's introduction to a Tokyo art association. Recipient and exact day not given.

add_entries.headline: Again asking Schnitzler for a Pentecost piece
add_entries.digest: Herzl asked Schnitzler once more for something for Pentecost. It need not be about Pentecost, or even be a story, but it had to arrive by 22 May, and he wanted a yes or no at once. Schnitzler published nothing in the paper that year. Two weeks later Herzl was in Constantinople for his audience with Sultan Abdülhamid II, still editing the feuilleton between missions.
add_entries.source_note: Herzl to Schnitzler, 3 May 1901, Schnitzler letters edition L03828 (Herzl, Briefe, Propyläen 1993, p. 210). Audience with the Sultan in May 1901 is standard Herzl biography. Paraphrased.

add_entries.headline: Leaving Japan with a new way of making prints
add_entries.digest: At the end of February 1901 Orlik left Japan for Vienna after about ten months, taking back the methods of Japanese colour woodcut. Over the next years he made the Japanese print a working tool for Vienna and Berlin, not only a collector's object, and he showed his Japanese work in both cities.
add_entries.source_note: Schirn Mag on Orlik (departure end of February 1901). Later exhibitions are summarised, not dated here.

add_convergences.label: Japan at the Secession: the sixth exhibition
add_convergences.note: The collector, the critic and the traveller look at the same art from three distances. Fischer lends it and explains ukiyo-e in the catalogue. Bahr, in the Secession's own rooms, praises Japan's restraint and warns against borrowing without a purpose. Orlik leaves to learn the craft at its source, and finds the ports already westernised. The show drew the smallest crowds of any Secession exhibition, six weeks before Philosophy drew the largest storm.

add_convergences.label: Leutnant Gustl goes through the feuilleton editor's hands
add_convergences.note: Schnitzler's letters show the most subversive Viennese story of 1900 passing through Herzl's desk: offered as uncuttable, chased, printed at Christmas and then argued over for its fee. Herzl's diary of these months is about Zionism, not literature. To him the paper was a job, and to Schnitzler a venue.

add_ties.note: Old friends from 1890s literary Vienna. As feuilleton editor of the Neue Freie Presse, Herzl asked Schnitzler for pieces and printed Leutnant Gustl in the 1900 Christmas number.
Kraus mocked Herzl and Zionism in his 1898 pamphlet Eine Krone für Zion, and Die Fackel spent years attacking the Neue Freie Presse that Herzl wrote for.
In Japan in 1900 Fischer introduced Orlik to a Tokyo art association, which let him exhibit there.
Bahr's essay on the Japanese exhibition cites Fischer's book Wandlungen im Kunstleben Japans (1900).

add_threads_out.note: The Japanese prints Fischer lent the Secession in January 1900 reached European collectors in large numbers only after Perry's ships forced Japan open in 1853–54. Bahr's essay on the show dates the European fashion for Japan to the late 1860s and the Paris exhibition of 1867, and it notes that Japan, modernising after its revolution, now shared Europe's troubles.

fix.source_note: Publication in the NFP Christmas number 1900 is standard. Schnitzler's letters to Herzl of 15 November and 3 December 1900 and 14 January 1901 (Schnitzler letters edition L03937, L03935, L03940) confirm the offer for the Christmas number, the uncut printing and the fee dispute. The day of the issue was not checked against the paper.

updates.why: The Schnitzler–Herzl letters in the digital edition corroborate the Christmas-number placement. Confidence stays approx because the issue date was not checked.
